title: Trapping of nanofabricated SiO$_2$ high-aspect-ratio discs in an optical lattice
authors: Shelby Klomp, Shafaq Gulzar Elahi, Scott Grudichak, Chethn Galla, Zhiyuan Wang, Mark Nguyen, George Winstone, Katarina Boskovic Guy, Emma Derrick, Maddox Wroblewski, Jacob Sprague, Andrew Laeuger, Jackson Larsen, Nancy Aggarwal, Shane L. Larson, Andrew A. Geraci
abstract: We describe the nanofabrication and loading of lithographically patterned, high aspect ratio $10$ $μ$m diameter silicon dioxide discs with thickness of $400$ nm into an optical standing wave trap in vacuum. We obtain motional spectra of the center of mass motion of the discs using a combination of interferometric and imaging methods. The method is capable of high-efficiency loading and optical trapping using small numbers of objects, of the order of a few particles, with customized geometries and sizes compatible with wafer scale nanofabrication methods. Disc-like particles in optical traps have been identified as promising candidates for detectors of high frequency gravitational waves or as sensitive accelerometers.
summary: This research details the successful trapping and characterization of motion for lithographically fabricated, high-aspect-ratio $\text{SiO}_2$ discs in an optical vacuum trap. By measuring the motional spectra, the authors demonstrate a robust platform for sensing, suggesting applications for next-generation detectors of high-frequency gravitational waves.
main_problem: The paper demonstrates the high-efficiency optical trapping and characterization of motion for nanofabricated, high-aspect-ratio $\text{SiO}_2$ discs in a vacuum environment.
main_result: They successfully trapped single particles and measured motional spectra, showing the method's potential for highly sensitive force/acceleration sensing, particularly for gravitational wave detection.
method: The study combines top-down lithographic nanofabrication with optical trapping in a vacuum, characterizing motion using a combination of interferometric and imaging detection methods.
model_or_system: The physical system involves disc-shaped $\text{SiO}_2$ particles ($\approx 10 \mu\text{m}$ diameter, $400 \text{nm}$ thick) trapped by a standing wave optical lattice. Theoretical calculations use SCUFF-EM to model optical forces, while experiments measure motional spectra.
key_observables: Motional spectra peaks corresponding to translational ($x, y, z$) and librational ($\theta_x, \theta_y$) motion, and the figure of merit for thermal noise limited sensitivity ($\eta_{\text{thermal}}$).
important_parameters: Particle dimensions ($r \approx 4.5 \mu\text{m}$, $t = 400 \text{nm}$), trapping wavelength ($1560 \text{nm}$), and the deep Mie scattering regime ($k r \approx 20$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the deep Mie regime approximation for calculating optical forces and torques.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of the discs, the optical trapping apparatus setup, and amplitude spectral density plots comparing predicted motional peaks with measured spectra.
paper_structure: The paper details the nanofabrication process, describes the optical trapping setup, presents the theoretical modeling of forces, and reports on the experimental measurement and analysis of the motional spectra.
why_interesting: This work bridges nanofabrication, advanced optical trapping, and quantum sensing, directly impacting the field of optomechanics and high-precision measurement, which are core areas of AMO physics.

Figure 2. (upper) Diagram of the optical trapping apparatus consisting of a 1560 nm laser forming a dual-beam standing wave optical trap in a vacuum chamber. The motion of a disc is recorded by imaging the scattered trap light onto segmented quadrant photodiodes (QPD)s or by using a homodyne-like interference signal collected through the fiber onto a balanced detector [23]. A wave division multiplexer (WDM) allows the introduction of light at a separate wavelength which can be used for linear optical feedback cooling. (lower) Additonal SEM images of the discs.
